evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing on a case study of land occupations and informal settlements in the city of Belo Horizonte in Brazil, where the staples of life such as water, electricity, shelter and sanitation are co-constructed by the poor, the paper argues that infrastructures – visible and invisible – are deeply implicated in not only the making and unmaking of individual lives, but also in the experience of community, solidarity and struggle for recognition.

In this paper, I take up Larkin’s invitation to consider the poetics and politics of infrastructural visibility and invisibility by focusing on the struggle in poor informal urban settlements over staples generally available to the better-off elsewhere in a city.

My material is drawn from Belo Horizonte in Brazil, where I spent three weeks in August and September 2013 studying three organized land occupations by the poor, and also the favela of Nossa Senhora de Fátima, one of four favelas that make up the city’s largest and oldest informal settlement - Aglomerado da Serra – that houses 50,000 people, and where it has taken some 40 years for trunk infrastructures to become part of the invisible background of supply.

The long process of informal urbanisation tolerated by the authorities has eventually led to municipal upgrading of the favela’s trunk infrastructures and connectivity to the city’s water, electricity, sanitation, and transport system, along with better access to diverse social services.

In Aglomerado da Serra, the programme has seen work on some 850 new apartments by late 2013, many more demolitions and evictions from sites considered as environmentally risky or needed for infrastructural projects, and a set of communal interventions including social centres, green spaces, new trunk roads, paved pathways, and the linkage of houses to mains sanitation (figure 7).

criterion_notes.c1: Touches on household and community water and sanitation provisioning in informal settlements in Belo Horizonte (pirated water connections, household and shared Tevap sanitation pits in three new land occupations, and municipal mains water and sewage connectivity in Nossa Senhora de Fátima), though bundled with housing, electricity, roads, and communal spaces as material context rather than examined as a standalone WASH service-access study.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2: the paper examines the socio-material agency, aesthetics, and visibility/invisibility of physical infrastructure ('lively infrastructure'), alongside activist/architectural settlement layout models, generic municipal slum-upgrading project delivery (URBEL's Vila Viva apartment blocks, highway, gully fencing, and mains sanitation works), and unanalysed macro-governance background (courts, political cycles, clientelism, democratization). It does not analyse any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing water or sanitation access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules for utility connections, tariffs, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure). Under the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2, the paper discusses informal occupation self-governance and municipal slum-upgrading governance broadly, yet its actual independent variable is infrastructural visibility/materiality rather than a governance determinant of WASH access, and even if plain Criterion 2 were treated as generously satisfied, the study would still be excluded for lacking a water/sanitation access outcome (c4) and an identifiable empirical study design linking governance exposure to service access (c5).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative field observations drawn from a three-week visit by the author in August and September 2013 to three organized land occupations (Dandara, Eliana Silva, Rosa Leão) and one established favela (Nossa Senhora de Fátima) in Belo Horizonte, although presented as an interpretive theoretical essay without a formal methods section or systematic data-collection protocol.
criterion_notes.c4: The studied outcomes are urban sociality, affective dispositions, community solidarity and commoning ('infra-designation', 'infra-being', 'infra-commoning'), vernacular aesthetics, and citizenship subjectivity. Water and sanitation conditions (pirated water and sanitation pits versus municipal mains connectivity and erratic supply) are described solely as part of the infrastructural exposure/backdrop shaping sociality, not evaluated as outcomes of a legal or institutional factor.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the settlement sites in Belo Horizonte, but does not report an identifiable empirical study design, sampling or interview protocol, or a defined legal/governance exposure and water/sanitation access outcome at a clear unit of analysis.

study_design: Qualitative observational case vignettes within a social-theory essay (three-week field visit in August-September 2013; no formal methods section reported)
population_and_sample: Three organized urban land occupations (Dandara, ~1,200 households; Eliana Silva, ~300 families; Rosa Leão, ~1,300 families) and one favela (Nossa Senhora de Fátima, ~10,000 inhabitants, within Aglomerado da Serra, ~50,000 inhabitants) in Belo Horizonte; no individual or household sample reported
exposure: Visibility and invisibility ('liveliness') of self-built and municipal urban infrastructure (housing, 3D settlement layout models, pirated water/electricity, sanitation pits, trunk roads, and URBEL's Vila Viva slum-upgrading interventions)
outcome: Urban sociality, affective and sensory dispositions, community solidarity and commoning ('infra-designation', 'infra-being', 'infra-commoning'), vernacular aesthetics, and political subjectivity
rationale: Exclude (E03 - Wrong exposure). Although this cultural-geography essay draws on a three-week field visit to three land occupations and one favela in Belo Horizonte where pirated water, sanitation pits, and municipal mains water/sanitation connections are part of the built environment, its analytical exposure is the materiality and visibility/invisibility of physical infrastructure itself ('lively infrastructure'), alongside self-build architectural layout models, generic municipal slum-upgrading project delivery (URBEL's Vila Viva housing, highway, gully fencing, and mains sanitation works), and unanalysed macro-governance commentary. It does not examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing water or sanitation service access (c2=no). Moreover, its causal direction is inverted relative to the review: water/sanitation infrastructure serves as part of the socio-technical exposure shaping urban sociality, commoning, and affect rather than an evaluated service-access outcome (c4=no), and no structured empirical study design or data-collection protocol is reported (c5=no). Consequently, it is also excluded under the plain wording of Criterion 2.
